Sampled-negative HR@10 can disagree with full-catalog ranking, including reversing model comparisons; large sampled margins therefore do not establish strong catalog retrieval. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) establish this inconsistency; [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) further evaluates sampling fidelity, resolution and exposure-bias robustness. Keep the pinned 99-negative evaluator for selection, while separately measuring full-catalog unseen-item target rank and top-10 hits on a small, fixed validation subset. Treat agreement between diagnostics and validation improvements as an empirical question.

Temporal diagnostics require careful interpretation. [Time to Split (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748164) finds that per-user leave-one-out can distort model rankings through global temporal leakage. Training-history prefix probes can reveal sensitivity to context length and recency without changing benchmark splits, but withheld prefix targets already seen during fitting measure reconstruction, not generalization. [A 2024 reproduction study](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/33989/) also identifies user grouping and evaluation strategy as factors affecting popularity-bias conclusions. Report diagnostic hits by training-derived item-frequency and history-length bins, alongside recommendation coverage and head-item concentration.

Suggested uncertainty procedure: paired user bootstrap of candidate-minus-baseline hit indicators, resampling within each category and recomputing the four-category macro-average; report a 95% interval and subgroup counts. This estimates uncertainty conditional on fixed users/candidates and trained models, not training-seed variability or search-selection bias. These are proposed supporting diagnostics—not established predictors of HR@10 gains. Calibrate them against observed validation changes; retain the fixed macro HR@10 selection criterion and one trained BERT4Rec model per category.
